system: Vedic horā (Tier A) and Choghadiya (Tier C) — two divisions of the sunrise-bounded Indian civil day. Both are living practice; both are described here, never prescribed, and no claim of predictive or operative validity is made or implied.
compiledBy: COMPILER role, under docs/plans/horae/RESEARCH-PROTOCOL.md C3 (fetcher/compiler split). This file cites ONLY snippet ids present in the round-2 fetcher ledger. No source was introduced by the compiler, and no citation was written from the compiler's own knowledge. Every arithmetic derivation in this file was re-run against the ledger cells before it was written down.
scopeNote: horā here means the HOUR, not the half-sign / D-2 varga. Al-Bīrūnī records both senses of the word side by side (S3-d) and this dossier covers only the first. No jyotiṣa text asserting the half-sign sense was fetched, so none is cited.
dayStart: SUNRISE, for both systems, with the civil day running sunrise to sunrise. Tier A: the Sūrya Siddhānta defines the civil (sāvana) reckoning by counting sunrises (S1-c); and al-Bīrūnī, quoting Vijayanandin's Karaṇatilaka, reckons the hour-lord by adding the signs risen "since the morning" (S3-j). Tier B: the 1860 translator's note to i.12–13 states that the civil day is the natural day, counted in India from sunrise to sunrise (S2-a). Tier C, current practice: the pañcāṅga day starts and ends with sunrise (S7-c), and the horā day is the duration from one sunrise to the next (S7-a). FOR CHOGHADIYA SPECIFICALLY the two boundaries are sunrise and sunset: the sunrise-to-sunset span is the day Choghadiya and the sunset-to-next-sunrise span is the night Choghadiya (S4-a). A CAVEAT ROUND 1 WAS PULLED UP FOR AND THIS ROUND KEEPS: nothing at Sūrya Siddhānta xii.78–79 or i.51 mentions sunrise. The sunrise anchor comes from i.12 (S1-c) and from the translator's note (S2-a), and it is cited to those and not to the hour-lord verses.
divisionRule: HORĀ — TWO READINGS, BOTH KEPT. (a) SEASONAL, twelve by day and twelve by night [Tier A, al-Bīrūnī c. AD 1030 / Sachau 1910]: the dominants are arranged according to the horæ temporales (S3-g); each day and each night has twelve hours (S3-h); the hours used in the theory of the dominants are horæ obliquæ temporales (S3-i). Tier C current practice states the same and can be measured off the rendered tables: twelve each in day and night, each arc divided into twelve equal parts (S8-a), giving 72.5-minute day horās against 47.583-minute night horās on one date (S7-d, S7-e) and 67.5 against 52.5 at another location on the same date (S8-e). (b) A TWENTY-FOURTH OF THE DAY [Tier B, the 1860 translator's notes]: the division of the day into twenty-four hours, each assigned in succession to the planets (S2-b), and the hours, or twenty-fourths of the day (S2-h). The fetcher records that this 1/24 wording is the translator's own gloss and not wording in the Sanskrit verse, and the Sanskrit was never retrieved. One Tier C source states 24 horās in a day of approximately one hour each and then retracts the approximation in its own next sentence, tying it to the sunrise-to-sunrise total (S8-d). RULER SEQUENCE, and this part is not in dispute anywhere in the ledger: the regents run in downward order from Saturn (S1-h) through the order Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon (S1-d, S1-e; restated at S2-c and, as "from above to below", at S3-k); the first horā of a weekday belongs to that weekday's lord (S2-e, S2-i; Tier C S7-f, S8-b, S8-c); and the weekday lords themselves are got by taking every fourth planet downward from Saturn (S1-f), which reproduces Saturday, Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday exactly. The cycle crosses sunset without resetting (S7-e, S8-e), which is the behaviour al-Bīrūnī describes at S3-c. CHOGHADIYA — one rule, agreed; the durations, not. The rule: the sunrise-to-sunset arc is divided into 8 and the sunset-to-sunrise arc into 8, sixteen in the nychthemeron (S4-b, S5-c, S6-c, S6-g, S10-d). The first division of each weekday is ruled by that weekday's lord (S4-d), the eighth division of the daytime repeats the day lord (S4-f), the sequence differs per weekday and is fixed for that weekday (S5-d), and seven names fill eight slots because one name takes two (S5-e). The five incompatible fixed-minute figures the same sources print alongside that rule are recorded under contestedPoints and are not adopted. THE NIGHT SEQUENCE DOES NOT CONTINUE THE DAY SEQUENCE — on all seven weekdays the observed night start differs from the cell a continuing cycle would reach — and NO SOURCE IN THIS LEDGER STATES A NIGHT-START RULE OR A REASON FOR THE OFFSET (see gaps). The closed forms that reproduce all 112 published cells are recorded in variants[V3].compilerDerivations, labelled in-data as the compiler's arithmetic.
rulerColumnJustification: TRUE, and asymmetrically — the two halves of this file do not carry the same weight and must not render as though they did. VEDIC HORĀ, TIER A: a primary text assigns a governing planet to each division. Sūrya Siddhānta xii.79 states that the regents of the hours occur in downward order from Saturn (S1-h); xii.30–31 supply that downward order (S1-d, S1-e); xii.78 derives the weekday regent by the same descent (S1-f). This is the one genuine Tier A ruler column in the Horae Mundi grid. CHOGHADIYA, TIER C ONLY: four commercial almanacs assign a planet to each of the seven names (S4-g through S4-m and S5-h through S5-n) and agree on all seven, but no primary text and no peer-reviewed scholarship supports them anywhere in this ledger. PER THE MAINTAINER'S GRID RULING, zmanim, shichen, Egyptian and Babylonian have no ruler column at all, and nothing in this file offers one for them. The asymmetry is the teaching. One further limit, from the ledger and not from taste: the horā divisions carry NO quality grade in this ledger, and four of the seven Choghadiyas carry none either — those cells are empty and the gaps entry says how hard was looked.

variants.label: Two hour-lord computation rules distinct from plain counting from sunrise
variants.whatItIs: Al-Bīrūnī records two ascendant-based procedures for the dominus horae, neither of which is the simple "count planets from sunrise" rule the Tier C almanacs use.
variants.ruleOne: From an Indian astronomical handbook al-Bīrūnī does not name: divide the distance between the sun and the degree of the ascendant, in equal degrees, by 15 and add 1 to the quotient (S3-e).
variants.ruleTwo: From Vijayanandin's Karaṇatilaka, named: add the signs risen since the morning to the degree of the horoscope (S3-j), then count the quotient off from the dominant of the nychthemeron, taking the planetary spheres from above to below (S3-k) — the same descending order as Sūrya Siddhānta xii.31 (S1-e). Al-Bīrūnī adds that Vijayanandin ought to have said "add one" to the quotient.
variants.whyItMatters: Karaṇatilaka is the only named Indian text in this ledger, other than the Sūrya Siddhānta, that states an hour-lord rule; and it reckons from "the morning", i.e. sunrise.

variants.label: The observed 7-weekday Choghadiya table, as published — 112 cells
variants.whatItIs: The directly-observed data. Every cell below was read off a rendered or static table in the ledger; nothing here is interpolated. Two independent witnesses cover all seven weekdays (DrikPanchang dated pages S4-n…S4-u; mPanchang static tables S5-a, S5-b, first row only), and a third covers Saturday in full (AstroSage S6-a, S6-b). attestedRules: The first division of each weekday is ruled by that weekday's lord (S4-d), worked for Sunday at S4-e.
The last division of the daytime is ruled by the day lord too (S4-f), which is why eight slots hold seven names.
The sequence differs per weekday and is fixed for that weekday (S5-d).
Seven names fill eight slots because six take one slot and one takes two (S5-e).

compilerDerivations.warning: THESE ARE ARITHMETIC OVER THE CELLS ABOVE, NOT STATEMENTS ANY SOURCE MAKES. They reproduce all 112 published cells with zero failures and are recorded so a renderer can be tested against them; they must never be presented as sourced.
compilerDerivations.dayRule: Start on the weekday lord and step +1 through the descending list; the 8th cell repeats the 1st.
compilerDerivations.nightRule: Step −2 through the same list; the 8th cell repeats the 1st.
compilerDerivations.nightStartRule: The night sequence starts on the lord of the fifth weekday counted inclusively from the current one — equivalently, five places on in the descending list from the day's starting cell. Verified on all seven weekdays.
compilerDerivations.weekdayStep: Both the day-start and the night-start advance three places along the descending list from one weekday to the next.
compilerDerivations.resetAtSunset: The night sequence does NOT continue the day sequence: on every one of the seven weekdays the observed night start differs from the cell the day cycle would have reached. This is the point of contrast with the horā, which does continue (S7-e).

honestLimits: WHAT THIS FILE IS. A round-2 compilation from a fetcher ledger of ten sources. Every row carries at least one snippet id; no source was introduced; nothing was cited from the compiler's own knowledge. Round 1 pinned 21% of its claims to sources that did not support them, and three of six dossiers invented a confirmed gap; the constraints below exist because of that, and are worth reading as limits rather than as throat-clearing. THE TIER A FLOOR IS THINNER THAN IT LOOKS. Two Tier A sources carry this system: the Sūrya Siddhānta in Burgess's 1860 translation (S1) and al-Bīrūnī in Sachau's 1910 translation (S3). The Sanskrit of xii.78–79 was never retrieved — both GRETIL URLs 404'd — so the claim that the verse uses the word horā rests on a parenthetical transliteration inside a Victorian English translation whose two independent OCR scans both lose the macron. The 1860 translator's own note says that, apart from that passage and its parallel, the Sūrya Siddhānta makes no reference to the week at all (S2-j), which is a fair measure of how thin the attestation inside that text is. THERE IS NO MODERN SCHOLARSHIP IN THIS FILE. Pingree's Yavanajātaka and Jyotiḥśāstra — the standard Tier B treatments — were not fetched and are cited nowhere. The only Tier B material is a 166-year-old translator's annotation which al-Bīrūnī partly contradicts. Consequently this dossier reports NO modern consensus on the Greek-loanword question or on anything else, and its silence on that should not be read as agreement with the 1860 position. CHOGHADIYA IS TIER C THROUGHOUT AND ITS PROVENANCE IS THE WEAKEST THING HERE. Four commercial almanacs and one encyclopedia article whose sole reference is a glossary of Buddhist terms, which itself contains no rulers and no weekday table and has carried an unsourced-article template since July 2012. No primary text, no scholarship, no date, no author, and one undated clause about western India. Meanwhile the DATA is the best-verified in the file: 112 published cells, three witnesses, zero disagreement, and boundary arithmetic that reproduces to the printed minute. Thin provenance plus rich data is the combination FRAMING flags as an evidential-dignity risk, because a well-cited apparatus lends its neighbours credibility they did not earn. WHAT IS DERIVED RATHER THAN SOURCED. The +1 day step, the −2 night step, the fifth-weekday-lord night start, the three-place weekday advance, and the observation that Choghadiya resets at sunset while the horā does not, are ALL the compiler's arithmetic over the published cells. They reproduce every one of the 112 cells, and they are stated by nobody. They live in variants[V3].compilerDerivations behind an explicit warning field, and they are not repeated in any field a renderer would read as sourced. WHAT IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT. No nameOriginal on any entry — the ledger contains no Devanāgarī or IAST for any individual division, and round 1 was pulled up for supplying them. No quality grade on any horā entry, and none on four of the seven Choghadiyas, because the ledger grades only three. No comparison row between the horā and the day-Choghadiya, although the arithmetic relation is visible, because no source in the ledger makes the comparison and FRAMING §2.4 forbids the site making it. No three-way split on Char's auspiciousness, though round 1 found one, because the snippets that would carry it are not in this ledger. SOURCES USED FOR NOTHING. S9 (Prokerala) came back through an extraction model rather than being read directly, so it is marked secondHand in sources[] and is cited in no entry and no golden value. S8-f, the unattributed Sanskrit verse, supports no row. S10 (Wikipedia) is CC BY-SA, which is not among the four verdicts FRAMING §4.1 permits for reproduction, so it is treated as cite-only. QUOTATION POLICY IN THIS FILE. S1, S2 and S3 are pd-us on a stated pre-1931 ground and may be quoted. S4 through S10 are cite-only; the verbatim strings in sources[] are the ≤25-word verification extracts the research protocol requires, they exist so a reviewer can check a citation without re-fetching, and they must not travel into shipped data. The companion notes file paraphrases those sources rather than quoting them. NO EFFICACY CLAIM IS MADE ANYWHERE. Words like auspicious, benefic and malefic in this file are the sources' own vocabulary, reported as their vocabulary, and are not endorsed.

contestedPoints: DIVISION OF THE HORĀ — seasonal or a plain twenty-fourth? BOTH POSITIONS STAND. (a) SEASONAL, Tier A: al-Bīrūnī (c. AD 1030, trans. Sachau 1910) reports that Indian astrologers arrange the dominants according to the horæ temporales (S3-g), that each day and each night has twelve hours (S3-h), and concludes that the hours used in the theory of the dominants are horæ obliquæ temporales (S3-i). (b) A TWENTY-FOURTH OF THE DAY, Tier B: the 1860 translator's notes speak of the division of the day into twenty-four hours with each assigned in succession to the planets (S2-b) and of the hours, or twenty-fourths of the day (S2-h). The fetcher records that this 1/24 formulation is the translator's own gloss at his note to xii.78–79 and is NOT wording in the Sanskrit verse — and the Sanskrit was never retrieved. NOTE THE TIER SHIFT AGAINST ROUND 1: round 1 put the seasonal reading at Tier C and the 24th at Tier A; on this ledger it is the other way round, because al-Bīrūnī is Tier A and says seasonal, and the 24th is a Tier B annotation glossing a verse nobody in this round read. The two are not the same arithmetic: seasonal day-horās and night-horās differ in length on the same date at every latitude except at equinox, which the retrieved tables show directly (72.5 min by day against 47.583 by night, S7-d/S7-e; 67.5 against 52.5 at a second location, S8-e).

DID INDIANS USE HOUR-LORDS AT ALL? BOTH POSITIONS STAND, and they are 830 years apart. Burgess, writing in 1860, asserts that they never made that division of the day into twenty-four hours upon which the order of regency depends (S2-f). Al-Bīrūnī, writing c. AD 1030, reports that nobody in India uses the hours except the astrologers, for they speak of the dominants of the hours (S3-f) — and quotes a named Indian text, Vijayanandin's Karaṇatilaka, giving the rule (S3-j, S3-k). The fetcher flags this conflict explicitly. It is not resolved here.

THE ETYMOLOGY OF horā. Burgess (1860, Tier B) holds that the name by which the hours are there called (horā — ὥρα) indicates beyond a question the source whence they derived it (S2-g) — a Greek-loanword claim. A contemporary almanac (Tier C) states the indigenous derivation instead, deriving horā from (a)horā(tra), the duration from one sunrise to the next (S7-a). Both are printed here, dated and tiered. NO MODERN SCHOLARSHIP ON THIS QUESTION IS IN THIS LEDGER — see gaps — so this dossier reports no consensus, current or otherwise, and a reader should not read the 1860 position as the settled one merely because it is the older and more emphatic.

THE LENGTH OF A CHOGHADIYA — five different figures, one of them arithmetically wrong. Ninety-eight minutes (S10-a, on a footnote that could not be opened); ninety-six minutes (S10-b, and S4-c which hedges with "approximates"); ninety-six minutes AND one and a half hours in consecutive sentences of the same FAQ (S5-g); 90.125 minutes (S10-c); ninety minutes (S6-c); and "about 4 hours" (S6-d, where 3.75 ghaṭī is in fact 90 minutes). Three of these five appear on ONE page (S10-a, S10-b, S10-c). Structurally none of them is a length: every source that states the RULE states a proportional one — the sunrise-to-sunset arc divided by 8 (S4-b, S5-c, S6-c, S10-d) — so the fixed figures are all idealisations of a 12-hour day. The observed tables bear that out: 108.75 min by day and 71.375 by night on one date (S4-n, S4-o), 101.25 and 78.75 on the same date elsewhere (S6-a, S6-b).

THE ETYMOLOGY DOES NOT MATCH THE ARITHMETIC, in the sources' own numbers. The name is glossed as cho (four) + ghaḍiyā (ghaṭī), four ghaṭī (S4-c, S10-b). But the same sources divide 30 ghaṭī by 8 (S4-b, S5-f, S10-d), which is 3.75 ghaṭī, and AstroSage says 3.75 outright (S6-d). DrikPanchang alone marks the gap, writing that each muhūrta "approximates to" four ghaṭī (S4-c). Recorded, not resolved. Note also that only S5-g ties a ghaṭī to minutes at all, and it does so inconsistently.

DOES THE NIGHT GET ITS OWN LORD? Al-Bīrūnī (Tier A) draws the distinction himself: Greek and Muslim practice gives the night a separate lord, whereas the Hindus make the dominus diei the dominus of the whole nychthemeron, so that day and night follow each other (S3-c). CAUTION CARRIED FROM THE FETCHER: S3-a and S3-b describe MUSLIM astronomers' practice, not Indian, and must not be attributed to India on their own. Tier C current practice matches al-Bīrūnī on the horā — the cycle crosses sunset without resetting, Venus being followed by Mercury (S7-e, S8-e). Choghadiya behaves the OPPOSITE way in the published tables: its night sequence starts somewhere the day sequence would not have reached, on every one of the seven weekdays. That contrast is recorded as an observation over the cited cells; no source in this ledger comments on it.

THE HOUR-NAMES ARE A SEPARATE LAYER FROM THE RULERS, and al-Bīrūnī says where he thinks they come from with his own hedge attached: "We think they are taken from the book Śrudhava" (S3-o). The twelve day-names and twelve night-names (S3-m, S3-n) carry a Lucky/Unlucky column of their own that has no relation to the planetary regents. They are recorded under variants[V1] rather than merged into entries[], because merging them would produce a composite table that neither the Sūrya Siddhānta nor al-Bīrūnī prints. Sachau's own "(?)" marks on four night-names are carried through unchanged.

CHAL, CHAR, CHARA OR CHANCHAL — and Kaal or Kala, Shubh or Shubha or Shoobh, Amrit or Amrita or Amrut, Labh or Labha or Laabh, Rog or Roga, Udveg or Udvega. All are printed; no source in this ledger adjudicates, and no Devanāgarī or IAST form is given for any of them. Every attested spelling is recorded per entry with its sid, and the display form is flagged in-data as an editorial choice rather than a philological claim. A NOTE ON WHAT IS *NOT* HERE: round 1 reported a three-way split on Char's auspiciousness across four sources. This ledger contains a quality verdict for Char from ONE source only (S4-h, auspicious). The three-way split is therefore not reported here — not because it is wrong, but because the snippets that would carry it were not fetched this round.

THE AUTHORSHIP OF THE 1860 ANNOTATIONS IS ITSELF UNSETTLED HERE. This ledger labels S2 "Ebenezer Burgess, translator's notes and commentary", and this dossier follows the ledger. The repository's own phase-1 report attributes the same annotations to Whitney. Nothing in this ledger resolves which, and no snippet bears on it. Wherever the attribution is load-bearing this file says "the 1860 translation's translator's notes" and names the ledger's attribution alongside; anyone building on it should settle the question from the title page before printing a name.

THE ARITHMETIC RELATION BETWEEN THE DAY-CHOGHADIYA AND THE HORĀ IS DELIBERATELY NOT PRINTED AS A ROW. Both start on the weekday lord and both step the same direction through the same seven-planet list; one divides by eight, the other by twelve. NO SOURCE IN THIS LEDGER MAKES THAT COMPARISON, and FRAMING §2.4 says that where no scholar has made the comparison there is no row. The observation is recorded here, in the contested-points prose, as a thing a future round would need a named source for — not as a finding, and not in any machine-readable field a renderer could pick up.

THE RULER COLUMN IS TIER A BUT ITS WEEKDAY LABELS ARE TIER C. The Sūrya Siddhānta gives the ordered sequence of regents — every fourth planet downward from Saturn (S1-f) — and the 1860 notes anchor it and demonstrate it across three consecutive days (S2-c, S2-d, S2-e, S2-i). Neither names an English weekday. The mapping Sun–Sunday, Moon–Monday, Mars–Tuesday, Mercury–Wednesday, Jupiter–Thursday, Venus–Friday, Saturn–Saturday is stated in this ledger only by a commercial almanac (S8-g), with the same anchors restated one by one on a second (S7-f). The sequence is Tier A; the labels on it are Tier C, and a renderer that prints "Saturday: Saturn" is combining the two.

THE TWO SYSTEMS MUST NOT RENDER AT THE SAME WEIGHT. Vedic horā has a Tier A ruler column resting on a primary text. Choghadiya has a Tier C ruler column resting on four commercial almanacs, with no primary text, no scholarship, no date and no named author. The data quality runs the opposite way to the provenance quality: the Choghadiya table is the best-verified thing in this file (112 cells, three witnesses, zero disagreement) and the worst-provenanced. That combination is the one FRAMING warns about by name under evidential dignity, and it is why the Tier C label has to travel on the comparison view itself and not merely as a badge.
